entry: Feeding of an [[Infant|infant]] with breast milk, directly from the breast or with milk expressed by a breast pump. The [[World Health Organization|World Health Organization]] (WHO) recommends that breastfeeding begin within the first hour after birth and continue as the baby wants, with exclusive breastfeeding for six months, followed by complementary foods and breastfeeding for up to 2 years and beyond. Exclusive breastfeeding rose from 37.0% to 47.4% between 2012 and 2024. Breastfeeding reduces the risk of respiratory tract infections, ear infections, sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) and [[Diarrhea|diarrhea]] in babies. Increased breastfeeding in low- and middle-income countries could prevent approximately 820,000 deaths of children under five annually. For mothers, it reduces blood loss after delivery and the risk of postpartum depression, and over the long term, the risk of [[Breast cancer|breast cancer]], [[Cardiovascular disease|cardiovascular disease]] and [[Rheumatoid arthritis|rheumatoid arthritis]]. Medical conditions that prevent breastfeeding are rare.

Rhythmic process of inhaling [[Oxygen|oxygen]]-rich air into the [[Lung|lungs]] and exhaling carbon dioxide, enabling gas exchange. All aerobic organisms require oxygen for [[Cellular respiration|cellular respiration]], which produces carbon dioxide as a waste product. In [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] with lungs, breathing consists of repeated cycles of inhalation and exhalation through a branched system of airways that lead to the alveoli, where gases move by [[Diffusion|diffusion]]. The [[Circulatory system|circulatory system]] transports the gases between the lungs and the tissues. Under normal conditions, homeostatic mechanisms control the depth and rate of breathing unconsciously, maintaining arterial partial pressures of carbon dioxide and oxygen and thereby keeping extracellular fluid pH stable. Breathing also supports speech and reflexes such as yawning and coughing, and contributes to [[Thermoregulation|thermoregulation]], as in panting. The lungs expand mainly through contraction of the diaphragm and, to a lesser extent, the intercostal muscles, while exhalation at rest is largely passive.

French New Wave crime drama directed by [[Jean-Luc Godard|Jean-Luc Godard]]. *Breathless* (*À bout de souffle*, lit. "Out of Breath") stars Jean-Paul Belmondo as Michel, a wandering criminal, and Jean Seberg as his American girlfriend, Patricia. It was Godard's first feature-length film and brought Belmondo his breakthrough as an actor. The film is an influential example of French New Wave cinema. Along with [[François Truffaut|François Truffaut]]'s *The 400 Blows* and Alain Resnais's *Hiroshima mon amour*, both released a year earlier, it brought international attention to new French filmmaking styles. Its bold visual style included unconventional jump cuts. On its initial release in France, it attracted over two million viewers. A fully restored version was released in the United States in May 2010 to mark the film's 50th anniversary. Critic Pauline Kael called it the most important New Wave film to reach the United States.

Clastic rock of angular, coarse fragments bound by a finer-grained matrix or cement. Unlike [[Conglomerate (geology)|conglomerate]], whose clasts are rounded, breccia contains at least 30 percent [[Gravel|gravel]]-sized particles over 2 mm with sharp edges that have not been worn down, indicating deposition close to the source. Sedimentary breccias form by sedimentary processes, such as scree cemented at the base of a cliff. Fault or tectonic breccias result from the grinding of two fault blocks as they slide past each other. Volcanic breccias form by explosive eruption of lava and other rock. Megabreccias, with fragments from at least 1 meter to more than 400 meters, can form through [[Landslide|landslides]], [[Impact event|impact]] events or [[Caldera|caldera]] collapse.

Group of domestic animals within a [[Species|species]] that share homogeneous appearance, behavior or other characteristics distinguishing them from other members of the species. Breeds form through genetic isolation and either natural adaptation or [[Selective breeding|selective breeding]], or both. No single scientifically accepted definition of the term exists; a breed is a term used among breeders for a nameable subset of a species. Individuals of a breed pass predictable traits to their offspring, a property called breeding true. Plant breeds are more commonly called [[Cultivar|cultivars]]. Offspring of animals from different breeds are crossbreeds or mixed breeds, and crosses above the breed level, such as between species, are [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrids]]. Breeders select foundation stock and mate the most desirable animals, and a breed standard describes desirable and undesirable traits. Populations must be large enough to maintain a breed without forced [[Inbreeding|inbreeding]].

[[Electromagnetic radiation|Electromagnetic radiation]] produced when a charged particle, typically an [[Electron|electron]], is deflected and decelerated by the field of another charged particle, usually an [[Atomic nucleus|atomic nucleus]]. The particle loses [[Kinetic energy|kinetic energy]], which is converted into [[Photon|photons]], in accordance with [[Conservation of energy|conservation of energy]]. The spectrum is continuous, becoming more intense and shifting toward higher frequencies as the energy change of the decelerated particles increases. More broadly, the term covers any radiation produced by acceleration of a charged particle, such as synchrotron radiation. Radiation from [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]] is called free-free radiation. In the narrower sense used most often, the term refers to radiation produced when electrons decelerate in matter, as in [[X-ray|X-ray]] tubes.

American novelist and screenwriter, a member of the Literary Brat Pack. His debut novel, *Less Than Zero* (1985), was followed by *American Psycho* (1991), his most successful novel, narrated by a [[Wall Street|Wall Street]] executive turned [[Serial killer|serial killer]]. The literary establishment widely condemned it as overly violent and misogynistic, and after publisher Simon & Schuster dropped it, Alfred A. Knopf released it in paperback. His later novels, such as *Lunar Park* (2005) and *The Shards* (2023), became increasingly metafictional. Four of his works have been filmed, including *American Psycho* (2000). He hosts a [[Podcast|podcast]].

Canadian [[Professional wrestling|professional wrestler]] known as the Hitman, and a member of the Hart wrestling family. He held five WWF Championships and two WCW World Heavyweight Championships, and he headed the Hart Foundation stable in the World Wrestling Federation (WWF, now [[WWE|WWE]]). He left for World Championship Wrestling (WCW) after the controversial Montreal Screwjob of November 1997. A concussion in December 1999 sidelined him, and he officially retired in October 2000. He was the first wrestler inducted three times into the WWE Hall of Fame. He later worked on stroke recovery and [[Cancer|cancer]] awareness.

American former professional football quarterback. He played 20 seasons in the [[National Football League|National Football League]] (NFL), mainly with the Green Bay Packers, who won [[Super Bowl|Super Bowl]] XXXI with him, the team's first championship in nearly three decades. He won three consecutive Most Valuable Player awards from 1995 to 1997 and had 321 consecutive starts from 1992 to 2010. He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2016. In 2022, investigations of the [[Mississippi|Mississippi]] welfare funds scandal determined that $8 million intended for welfare programs went to him or to causes he championed. Favre denied the allegations and filed a defamation lawsuit.

Process of producing [[Beer|beer]] by steeping a [[Starch|starch]] source, usually [[Cereal|cereal grains]] such as [[Barley|barley]], in water and fermenting the sweet liquid with [[Yeast|yeast]]. Brewing has taken place since at least the 11th millennium BC, and archaeological evidence indicates that prehistoric peoples and civilizations, including those of [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]], China and [[Mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], brewed beer. Major steps include malting, milling, mashing, boiling, fermenting, conditioning and packaging. Most beer is flavored with [[Hops|hops]]. There are three main fermentation methods: warm, cool and spontaneous. The earliest evidence of cereal-based beer comes from Raqefet Cave in present-day Israel, where the Natufians brewed beer around 13,000 years ago. A 3,900-year-old Sumerian poem honoring Ninkasi, the patron goddess of brewing, contains the oldest surviving beer recipe.

Withdrawal of the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]] (UK) from the [[European Union|European Union]] (EU), effective January 31, 2020. The UK was the only EU member state to leave. In a June 23, 2016, [[Referendum|referendum]], 51.9% of voters chose to leave. All regions of England and Wales except Greater London voted to leave, while Scotland and Northern Ireland voted to remain. Leave campaigners emphasized democratic accountability, and Remain campaigners warned of trade disruption and diminished global influence. The result led to the resignation of Prime Minister [[David Cameron|David Cameron]]. A transition period ended on December 31, 2020, and a trade agreement signed on December 30, 2020, set the future relationship.

English football player and manager, known for league titles with Derby County and Nottingham Forest. With his assistant Peter Taylor, he won two consecutive European Cups with Forest in 1979 and 1980. He was one of four managers to win the English league with two clubs. As a striker for Middlesbrough and Sunderland, he scored 251 league goals in 274 matches. He was never appointed England manager and was dubbed the "greatest manager England never had".

English physicist and musician. Cox is a professor of [[Particle physics|particle physics]] at the University of Manchester and is best known to the public as the presenter of [[BBC|BBC]] science programs, including *The Infinite Monkey Cage* and *Wonders of the Universe*. He is also the author of popular science books, including *The Quantum Universe* (2011). Before his academic career, he was a keyboardist for the bands Dare and D:Ream. [[David Attenborough|David Attenborough]] described him as the natural successor for the BBC's scientific programming.

American filmmaker and a major figure of the [[New Hollywood|New Hollywood]] generation, known for suspense and psychological thriller films. His breakthrough was *Carrie* (1976), an adaptation of [[Stephen King|Stephen King]]'s novel. Later commercial successes included *The Untouchables* (1987) and *Mission: Impossible* (1996). He paid homage to [[Alfred Hitchcock|Alfred Hitchcock]] in films such as *Obsession* (1976) and *Body Double* (1984). Critics have faulted his work for its violence and sexual content, while other critics, including [[Roger Ebert|Roger Ebert]] and Pauline Kael, have championed it. *Carrie* was inducted into the National Film Registry of the [[Library of Congress|Library of Congress]].

English musician, record producer and visual artist. Eno pioneered ambient music and coined the term for works he conceived to be "as ignorable as possible", including *Discreet Music* (1975) and *Ambient 1: Music for Airports*. He was a member of the glam rock band Roxy Music from 1971 to 1973. As a producer, he worked on the [[David Bowie|David Bowie]] albums *Low*, *Heroes* and *Lodger*, known as the Berlin Trilogy, and produced [[Talking Heads|Talking Heads]] albums including *Remain in Light* (1980). With Daniel Lanois, he produced the [[U2|U2]] albums *The Unforgettable Fire* and *The Joshua Tree* (1987), one of the highest-selling albums in history. He composed the startup music for Windows 95. He is an activist for humanitarian, environmental and anti-war causes, and a founding member of the Long Now Foundation.

English music entrepreneur and band manager. He ran his family's music shop in [[Liverpool|Liverpool]], where he showed a gift for spotting talent. He first met [[The Beatles|the Beatles]] at a lunchtime concert at the Cavern Club in 1961. Although he had no experience in artist management, he signed the group, insisted that they adopt a clean-cut image and secured a recording contract with EMI's Parlophone label. He managed the Beatles until his death. His other clients included Gerry and the Pacemakers and Cilla Black.

American musician, singer, songwriter and record producer who co-founded [[The Beach Boys|the Beach Boys]]. After signing with Capitol Records in 1962, he became the first pop musician credited for writing, arranging, producing and performing his own material. He wrote or co-wrote more than three dozen U.S. Top 40 hits, including the number-one singles "Surf City" (1963) and "Good Vibrations" (1966). He produced *Pet Sounds* (1966). He struggled with mental illness throughout his life. He completed a version of *Smile* in 2004, which earned him his greatest acclaim as a solo artist. He received two [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Awards]] and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame|Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1988.

Rectangular building unit, usually of [[Clay|clay]], used to build walls and other elements in [[Masonry|masonry]] construction. Bricks are joined with mortar, adhesives or by interlocking, and are laid in courses in patterns called bonds. Fired bricks, used since c. 4000 BC, are among the longest-lasting and strongest building materials. Air-dried mudbricks, which contain a binder such as straw, have an older history. The oldest bricks, shaped from mud and dating before 7500 BC, were found at Tell Aswad in the upper [[Tigris|Tigris]] region. Early bricks at [[Jericho|Jericho]] measured 400 mm × 150 mm × 100 mm. Between 5000 and 4500 BC, Mesopotamia discovered fired brick. Indus Valley cities built with bricks conforming to a 1:2:4 ratio of thickness, width and length.

American actress, singer and filmmaker. She achieved her breakthrough in the independent drama *Short Term 12* (2013). She won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Room* (2015), in which she played a kidnapping victim. She played Carol Danvers / Captain Marvel in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe|Marvel Cinematic Universe]], beginning with *Captain Marvel* (2019). Her feature directorial debut was the independent comedy-drama *Unicorn Store* (2017). She is a [[Gender equality|gender equality]] activist and an advocate for [[Sexual assault|sexual assault]] survivors.

American religious leader and politician. He was the second president of [[The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints|The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints]] from 1847 until his death. After the 1844 killing of [[Joseph Smith|Joseph Smith]], he led Latter-day Saints west to the Salt Lake Valley and founded [[Salt Lake City|Salt Lake City]]. He was the first governor of [[Utah|Utah]] Territory from 1851 to 1858. As governor, he allowed polygamy and supported slavery in the territory. During the Utah War, Utah militia members killed at least 120 members of an immigrant wagon train in the Mountain Meadows Massacre. Young surrendered in 1858 and resigned as governor.

Seaside resort in the city of Brighton and Hove, on the south coast of [[England|England]], 47 miles (76 km) south of [[London|London]]. The settlement is recorded in the [[Domesday Book|Domesday Book]] (1086). In the Georgian era, Brighton became a fashionable resort under the patronage of the Prince Regent, later [[George IV|King George IV]], who built the Royal Pavilion. The arrival of railways in 1841 made it a destination for day-trippers from London. In the 2021 census, 10.7% of residents aged 18 and over identified as gay, lesbian or bisexual, the highest share in the UK.

French actress, singer, model and [[Animal rights|animal rights]] activist. She gained international recognition in 1957 for *And God Created Woman* (1956) and became one of the best-known symbols of the [[Sexual revolution|sexual revolution]]. Philosopher [[Simone de Beauvoir|Simone de Beauvoir]] wrote an essay about her in 1959. She appeared in 47 films, recorded more than 60 songs and starred in [[Jean-Luc Godard|Jean-Luc Godard]]'s *Le Mépris* (1963). She was awarded the Legion of Honour in 1985. After retiring from acting in 1973, she campaigned for animal welfare and founded the Brigitte Bardot Foundation. She was fined twice for public insults and five times for inciting racial hatred, over comments about Muslims in France and about residents of [[Réunion|Réunion]].

High-concentration solution of salt in water, typically [[Sodium chloride|sodium chloride]]. The term covers salt solutions from about 3.5%, typical of seawater, up to about 26%, a saturated solution depending on temperature. Brine forms naturally through evaporation of saline groundwater and is produced in the mining of sodium chloride. It is used for [[Pickling|pickling]] and brining food, for de-icing roads, and in a range of technological processes. It is also a by-product of [[Desalination|desalination]] and requires wastewater treatment. Iodine, bromine and lithium are obtained from brines.

Capital and most populous city of [[Queensland|Queensland]], [[Australia|Australia]] (pop., 2025: 2.83 million). Its central business district lies on a peninsula of the Brisbane River about 15 kilometers (9 mi) from its mouth at Moreton Bay. Established as a penal settlement in 1824, the city became Queensland's capital in 1859, when the state separated from [[New South Wales|New South Wales]]. During [[World War II|World War II]], the Allied command in the South West Pacific was based in the city, with the headquarters of General [[Douglas MacArthur|Douglas MacArthur]]. The city hosted the 1982 Commonwealth Games, World Expo 88 and the 2014 G20 summit, and will host the 2032 Summer Olympics and Paralympics. South Bank's parklands attract an estimated 16 million visitors each year.

City and ceremonial county in South West [[England|England]] (pop., 2024: 494,399). Bristol received a royal charter in 1155 and became a major port and a starting point for early voyages to the New World. At the height of the [[Atlantic slave trade|Bristol slave trade]], from 1700 to 1807, more than 2,000 slave ships carried an estimated 500,000 people from Africa to [[Slavery|slavery]] in the Americas. The city's modern economy is built on creative media, electronics and aerospace industries. It has two universities: the University of Bristol and the University of the West of England.
